newsitem.title: USA: U.S., British airlines seek U.S. alliance approval.
newsitem.headline: U.S., British airlines seek U.S. alliance approval.

text.p: American Airlines and British Airways said Friday they formally asked the Transportation Department to approve their controversial plan to link trans-Atlantic passenger and cargo operations.
Will Ris, American's vice president for governmental affairs, told a news conference that, based on approvals of other alliances, he hoped to get clearance within 90 days.

American Chairman Robert Crandall, said progress was being made in reaching a U.S.-British free-market "open skies" aviation agreement, which the two countries have said was needed before alliance approval could be granted.
"Thus, this application is the next logical step in the process of securing all the needed regulatory approvals," he added in a statement.

The application requested antitrust immunity for the alliance so the two carriers could coordinate their passenger and cargo services between the United States and Europe and market the services jointly.
"An American-British Airways alliance will provide consumers with important new price, service and quality options in the global marketplace, and we're eager to move ahead," Crandall said.

British Airways Chief Executive Robert Ayling said in a statement, "Our filing today represents a significant milestone towards the launch of our alliance and the introduction of the great benefits it promises for all trans-Atlantic travellers."

He told Reuters in Bangalore in southern India he was "optimistic" the alliance could start by April, as planned. He was there accompanying British Prime Minister John Major on a visit to the Indian subcontinent.

Crandall said that "fairness" required U.S. approval because Washington had already approved other such alliances of U.S. carriers -- United Airlines, Delta Air Lines Inc. and Northwest Airlines Corp. -- with European carriers.
But the alliance has run into strong opposition from many U.S. carriers and British carrier Virgin Atlantic Airways.
They have said in filings with regulatory agencies in London and Washington that the link-up would stifle competition and give the two carriers more than 60 percent of U.S.-British traffic.

British Airways and American say the deal will increase competition because it will only go ahead if Britain and the United States reach an aviation pact allowing all U.S. airlines into Britain and London's Heathrow airport, Europe's most popular airport.

However, opposing carriers have cited British Airways domination of Heathrow and say that, for them to compete, British Airways would have to give up many of its coveted takeoff and landing slots at the airport.
Bilateral "open skies" talks, on and off for the past two years, are to be resumed in Washington on Feb. 4, with Heathrow access seen as a remaining stumbling block.
British regulators have said approval of the alliance was conditional on British Airways and American giving up 168 slots a week at Heathrow to other carriers.
David Holmes, British Airways' director of corporate resources in Washington, told the news conference that 168 was too many to give up -- but some opposing U.S. carriers said it was too few.
He said Heathrow slots were always becoming available for other carriers either through better slot allocation by the airport or by the sale of slots by airlines owning but not using them.
